deep.reconstruction:
OVERVIEW. The page continues the previous folio (modulus 5+8i, norm 89). For three more primary Gaussian primes it builds an index table to base 1+i and then looks up a sequence of small primary primes. Each modulus m is primary in Gauss's normalization: b even and a+b ≡ 1 (mod 4).
- m = -5+2i, p = 29
- m = 1+4i, p = 17
- m = 3+2i, p = 13
The whole page is the numerical groundwork for biquadratic residue characters, i.e. for verifying biquadratic reciprocity.

A. STRUCTURE OF EACH TABLE (m = π, p = N(π), π̄ its conjugate).
- Column 2 is (1+i)^k reduced mod π to a small Gaussian integer. For -5+2i: 1, 1+i, 2i, -2+2i, 1-2i (≡ -4), -2+i (≡ 3-i), -3-i, i (≡ -2-4i), -1+i, -2, -2-2i, 2+i (≡ -4i), -1-2i (≡ 1+3i), 1-3i, -1 (≡ 4-2i).
- Hence (1+i)^7 ≡ i, (1+i)^14 ≡ -1, and 1+i is a primitive root of order 28.
- For 1+4i: 1, 1+i, 2i, 2+i, -i, 1-i, 2, 1-2i, -1. So (1+i)^4 ≡ -i and the order is 16.
- For 3+2i: 1, 1+i, 2i, -i, 1-i, 2, -1. So (1+i)^3 ≡ -i and the order is 12.
- In each case only half the period is tabulated, since the second half is the negatives.
- Column 1 is x_k = π̄·(1+i)^k with real and imaginary parts reduced mod p (my identification, checked entry by entry). Examples:
  - -5-2i, -3-7i, 4-10i, 14-6i, then -9+8i (= 20+8i - 29), ..., up to 5+2i = -x_0.
  - 1-4i, 5-3i, 8+2i, 6-7i, ..., -1+4i.
  - 3-2i, 5+i, 4+6i, -2-3i, 1-5i, 6-4i, -3+2i.
- Purpose (mine): x ≡ 0 mod π̄, and x ≡ π̄(1+i)^k mod π. So for any Gaussian integer z, the reduction of π̄·z mod p equals ±x_k exactly when z ≡ (1+i)^k (mod π). That turns index-finding into a simple look-up of a pair of residues mod p.
- Column 3 equals c·k mod (p-1):
  - c = 7 for p = 13: 7, 2, 9, 4, 11, 6.
  - c = 7 for p = 17: 0, 7, 14, 5, 12, 3, 10, 1, 8. The '5' is overwritten but correct.
  - c = 23 for p = 89 on the previous page.
  - For p = 29 the column is just k.
  - In every case c^2 ≡ 1 mod (p-1). I could not determine with certainty what this auxiliary index represents.

B. LOOK-UPS (rows of four numbers).
- For each prime q ≡ 1 mod 4, written q = a^2+b^2 with a odd and b even (signs normalized so a+bi is primary), Gauss writes the four partial products and adds them in pairs.
- For m = -5+2i, row 1 is -5a, row 2 is +2b, row 3 is -2a, row 4 is -5b. This is (a+bi)(-5-2i), reduced mod 29.
- Pairs (a,b) used: (3,2), (1,4), (-5,2), (-1,6), (5,4), (7,2), (-5,6), (-3,8), (5,8), (9,4), (-1,10), (3,10); then (-7,8), (-11,4), (7,10), (11,6), (-13,2), (-9,10), (-7,12). These are all p ≡ 1 (mod 4) from 13 to 193 (q = 13, 17, 29, …, 113 in the first group, then 137, …, 193).
- Results, left column: -11+13, 3+7, 0 (q = 29 itself), -12+1, 12-1, -2+5, 8+9, 2-5, -9+8, -8-9, -4-19 (≡ -4+10), 5+2, then -7+3, 5+2, 14-6, -14+6, 11-13, 7-3, 1+12.
- The right column holds the same for the conjugate a-bi: 10+4, -13-11, -8-9, …, -10-4, -11+13, ….
- Matching against ±x_k gives the indices of a+bi mod -5+2i: 13→13, 17→15, 37→19, 41→5, 53→21, 61→25, 73→7, 89→4, 97→11, 101→16, 109→14.
- For m = 1+4i: rows a, 4b, -4a, b, i.e. (a+bi)(1-4i) mod 17.
  - (3,2)→-6+7, (1,4)→0, (-5,2)→3+5, (-1,6)→6-7, (5,4)→4+1.
  - (7,2)→-2+8, (-5,6)→2-8, (-3,8)→-5+3, (5,8)→3+5, (9,4)→8+2.
  - (-11,4)→5-3, (7,10)→-4-1, (11,6)→1-4, (-13,2)→-5+3, (-9,10)→-3-5, (-7,12)→7+6.
  - (-1,10)→5-3, (3,10)→-8-2, (-7,8)→8+2.
  - Each is followed by the conjugate-prime values, e.g. (7,-2)→-1+4, (-11,-4)→7+6, (3,-2)→-5+3, (5,-4)→6-7.
  - The resulting indices mod 1+4i include 13→11, 29→13, 37→3, 41→12, 53→14, 61→6, 73→9, 89→13, 97→2.
- For m = 3+2i: rows 3a, -2b, 2a, 3b, i.e. (a+bi)(3+2i) mod 13. Here the multiplier is π itself, so the conjugates of the results are looked up.
  - Primes 17, …, 113 give -5+1, -6-4, -2+3, -6-4, 4-6, -1-5, 1+5, -1-5, 6+4, 3+2, 2-3, 2-3.
  - The conjugate primes give -2+3, 2-3, -4+6, -3-2, ….
  - The final blocks re-list entries such as 6-4, -5-1, 1-5, -2-3, which are the table entries x_5, x_7, x_4, x_3.

C. SIDE COMPUTATIONS.
- 55+22i = -11·(-5-2i) ≡ -3-7i = x_1 mod 29, i.e. -11 ≡ 1+i mod (-5+2i).
- -33+22i = -11·(3-2i) ≡ 6-4i = x_5 mod 13, i.e. -11 ≡ 2 ≡ (1+i)^5 mod (3+2i).
- (1+4i)(3-2i) ≡ -2-3i = x_3 and (1-4i)(3-2i) ≡ -5-i = x_7 mod 13. So ind_{3+2i}(1+4i) = 3 and ind_{3+2i}(1-4i) = 7.
- The margin '+36 / 26' and the bottom '−1+i³ ≡ −i, 4 10 6 +2 +2' are unclear scratch work. '(16)' is the folio number.

D. WHAT IT SERVES. The quantities (1+i)^{(p-1)/4} are: -i for 3+2i, -i for 1+4i, i for -5+2i, -i for 5+8i. These agree with the supplementary law (1+i/π)_4 = i^{(a-b-b^2-1)/4}. The systematic indices of every small primary prime modulo each tabulated prime, for both π and π̄, are exactly the data needed to compare (π/λ)_4 with (λ/π)_4, i.e. an empirical test of the biquadratic reciprocity law.
errors: No genuine arithmetic errors were found in the parts checked; all table entries and the look-up products verified.
Mod 29, the value for (-1,10) is left as -4-19, which is only partially reduced (≡ -4+10). This is not an error.
Mod 17, the third-column entry for k=3 is overwritten; the final '5' = 7·3 mod 16 is consistent.
Transcription signs in the second 17-group (row '+28+20+12+20+36') must be -28, +20, +12, -20, -36 for the stated results to come out, which they do. The ink blots hide the minus signs.

results.what: 1+i is a primitive root modulo the Gaussian primes -5+2i, 1+4i and 3+2i, with complete index tables.
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones-style index tables; Jacobi, Canon Arithmeticus 1839, for rational primes)

results.what: Look-up device: tabulate π̄(1+i)^k mod p, so that the index of z mod π is read off from π̄z mod p.
results.modern_name: CRT isomorphism Z[i]/(p) ≅ Z[i]/(π) × Z[i]/(π̄) used for computing residue characters

results.what: Values of (1+i)^{(p-1)/4} mod π, consistent with the supplementary law for 1+i.
results.modern_name: Supplementary law of biquadratic reciprocity for 1+i

results.what: Systematic indices of all primary primes of norm up to 193 modulo several primary primes, for both π and π̄.
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (law found empirically c. 1813–1814; announced 1832; first published proofs by Jacobi in lectures and Eisenstein in 1844)

deep.surprise_reason: These are computational tables of the type Gauss is known to have made when discovering biquadratic reciprocity. The CRT look-up trick is a nice detail but is elementary.

checkable.asserts: Equals I, a Gaussian integer, so (1+i)^7 ≡ i mod -5+2i and 1+i has order 28 mod 29.
Is a Gaussian integer, so (1+i)^4 ≡ -i mod 1+4i.
Is a Gaussian integer, so (1+i)^3 ≡ -i mod 3+2i.

Gives [-I, -I, I, -I], matching (1+i)^{(p-1)/4} mod π in the tables (supplementary law).
